clinicalPearls: Most common cause of primary nephrotic syndrome in non-diabetic White adults, typically presenting with heavy proteinuria and edema but preserved renal function early on.
About 70-80% of primary (idiopathic) cases are associated with circulating anti-PLA2R antibodies; a minority have anti-THSD7A antibodies instead.
Always screen for an underlying secondary cause (malignancy, autoimmune disease, infection, or drug exposure) before labeling disease as primary/idiopathic, especially in patients over 50-60 years.

Follows a 'rule of thirds' natural history in untreated primary disease: roughly one-third spontaneously remit, one-third have persistent proteinuria with stable function, and one-third progress to kidney failure over years.

Renal vein thrombosis and other thromboembolic events are disproportionately common because of the profound hypercoagulable state associated with heavy proteinuria and urinary loss of anticoagulant proteins.
Microscopic hematuria may be present, but heavy nephritic-range findings (red cell casts, marked hematuria) suggest an alternative or superimposed diagnosis.

Immunofluorescence classically shows granular capillary loop deposits of IgG (often IgG4-dominant in primary disease) and C3, with electron microscopy showing subepithelial deposits and spike formation on the basement membrane.
Response to therapy is slow (months), so treatment decisions and reassessment of remission should be based on sustained trends in proteinuria rather than short-term fluctuations.
harrison.pathophysiology: Membranous nephropathy results from in-situ formation of immune complexes along the subepithelial aspect of the glomerular basement membrane, most often triggered by autoantibodies against a native podocyte antigen (chiefly PLA2R, less commonly THSD7A or other targets) or against a planted exogenous/tumor antigen in secondary forms. Complement activation at the site of deposits leads to podocyte injury, cytoskeletal disruption, and a marked increase in glomerular capillary wall permeability to protein without significant inflammatory cell infiltration. Ongoing antigen-antibody deposition drives basement membrane thickening and the characteristic 'spike and dome' appearance seen on silver-stained biopsy over time. This process explains the disease's predominantly nephrotic (rather than nephritic) presentation.
nonInfectiousMimics: Drug-induced membranous nephropathy (e.g., certain NSAIDs or other implicated agents)
Systemic lupus erythematosus (class V lupus nephritis)
additionalInvestigations: 24-hour urine protein or spot urine protein-to-creatinine ratio - quantify and monitor nephrotic-range proteinuria
Serum anti-PLA2R antibody titer - confirms primary autoimmune membranous nephropathy and aids in monitoring immunologic activity
Renal biopsy with light microscopy, immunofluorescence, and electron microscopy - establishes diagnosis and stages disease
Age-appropriate malignancy screening - excludes paraneoplastic secondary membranous nephropathy
Hepatitis B and C serologies, syphilis serology, ANA/anti-dsDNA, and complement levels - screen for secondary infectious or autoimmune causes
Serum albumin and lipid panel - assess severity of nephrotic syndrome and cardiovascular risk
Renal function tests (creatinine, eGFR) trended over time - monitor for progression
Doppler imaging or cross-sectional imaging of renal veins if clinical suspicion - evaluate for renal vein thrombosis in severe nephrotic syndrome
redFlags: Sudden worsening of renal function, flank pain, or asymmetric limb swelling suggesting renal vein thrombosis or other thromboembolic event
Rapidly progressive decline in eGFR or emergence of an active urinary sediment suggesting a superimposed crescentic or proliferative process
Severe nephrotic syndrome with albumin markedly low, raising risk of thrombosis, infection, and volume complications requiring closer monitoring
New signs pointing to occult malignancy or systemic autoimmune disease that would change management from primary to secondary disease pathway
Anasarca with respiratory compromise or signs of pulmonary embolism
pitfalls: Assuming all membranous nephropathy is primary/idiopathic without adequately excluding secondary causes, particularly malignancy in older patients
Making treatment decisions based on a single proteinuria measurement rather than sustained trends, given the naturally fluctuating course and slow treatment response
Overlooking the markedly elevated thromboembolic risk and failing to consider prophylactic anticoagulation in severe nephrotic syndrome
Misinterpreting a negative anti-PLA2R antibody test as excluding membranous nephropathy, since a meaningful subset of primary cases are antibody-negative or have other target antigens
harrison.prognosis: Renal outcomes are highly variable, with roughly equal proportions of patients undergoing spontaneous remission, persistent stable proteinuria, or progression to kidney failure over years if untreated; lower proteinuria, preserved renal function at diagnosis, and declining PLA2R antibody titers portend a better outcome, while persistent heavy proteinuria and reduced eGFR predict progression.
references: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine, 22e - Glomerular Diseases chapter, section on Membranous Nephropathy
